title: Reflexes & UMN Signs
keywords: reflex reflexes deep tendon reflex dtr jerk hammer babinski plantar hoffmann clonus umn lmn
summary: Elicit and grade every deep tendon reflex, use reinforcement, and recognise upper-motor-neuron signs — Babinski, Hoffmann, clonus and jaw jerk.
ur: Har tendon reflex sahi elicit karna aur 0 se 4+ grade karna, aur UMN signs (Babinski, Hoffmann, clonus) identify karna.

sources.title: Lindsay, Bone & Fuller — Neurology and Neurosurgery Illustrated

goals.beginner: Know each reflex, its root and the normal response.
goals.intermediate: Elicit reflexes reliably, with reinforcement, and grade 0–4+.
goals.advanced: Interpret reduced and brisk reflexes and UMN signs.
goals.expert: Localise lesions — root, cord, brainstem — from reflex patterns.

concepts.title: The reflex arc in one breath
concepts.body: Tapping the tendon stretches the muscle spindle → sensory signal enters the cord → synapses with the motor neuron → the muscle contracts. Damage anywhere in the arc (root, nerve, muscle) **reduces** the reflex; loss of the brain's inhibition from above (UMN lesion) makes it **brisk**.
concepts.ur: LMN/root lesion = reflex kam; UMN (brain/cord) lesion = reflex brisk.

concepts.title: Six reflexes, six levels
concepts.body: Count up the body: **1, 2** (S1–S2) Achilles · **3, 4** (L3–L4) knee · **5, 6** (C5–C6) biceps and brachioradialis · **7, 8** (C7–C8) triceps. Add the medial hamstring for **L5**.
concepts.ur: Chhe reflexes, chhe levels: jism par upar ginein: 1, 2 (S1–S2) Achilles · 3, 4 (L3–L4) knee · 5, 6 (C5–C6) biceps aur brachioradialis · 7, 8 (C7–C8) triceps. Medial hamstring L5 ke liye add karein.

concepts.title: Grading 0 to 4+
concepts.body: Grade each reflex and always compare sides.

head: Grade
Meaning
rows: Brisk, more than average (may spread); can be normal if symmetrical
Very brisk with sustained clonus — abnormal

concepts.ur: Grading 0 se 4+: har reflex ko grade karein aur hamesha sides compare karein. 0 absent, 1+ kam (diminished), 2+ normal, 3+ brisk, 4+ bohat brisk clonus ke saath. Asymmetry numbers se zyada ahem hai.

concepts.title: Technique that works
concepts.body: Relax the muscle completely, put the tendon on slight stretch and let the hammer **swing freely** from the wrist. Tap the tendon (or your thumb on it) briskly. Compare sides at the same strength.
bullets: **Reinforcement (Jendrassik)**: ask the patient to hook the fingers together and pull, or clench the teeth, as you tap.
Watch and feel — some responses are easier to feel than to see.
concepts.ur: Muscle bilkul relaxed ho, hammer ko freely swing hone dein, aur dono sides par same force se tap karein.

concepts.title: Upper motor neuron signs
concepts.body: When the corticospinal pathway is damaged above the anterior horn cell you may find: **brisk reflexes**, **clonus**, an **extensor plantar response (Babinski)**, a **Hoffmann sign**, **spasticity** and a **pyramidal pattern** of weakness.
concepts.ur: Upper motor neuron signs: jab corticospinal pathway anterior horn cell se upar kharab ho to yeh mil sakte hain: brisk reflexes, clonus, extensor plantar response (Babinski), Hoffmann sign, spasticity aur kamzori ka pyramidal pattern.

concepts.title: Interpreting reflexes
concepts.body: One reduced reflex with matching weakness and numbness = root. Generally reduced reflexes, distal first (ankles) = polyneuropathy. Brisk reflexes **below** a level with normal ones above = cord lesion at that level. Brisk everywhere including the jaw = lesion above the pons.
concepts.ur: Reflexes ka matlab: ek reflex kam + usi level ki kamzori aur numbness = root. Aam taur par reflexes kam, pehle door wale (ankles) = polyneuropathy. Ek level se neeche brisk aur upar normal = cord lesion usi level par. Har jagah brisk, jaw samet = pons se upar lesion.

concepts.title: Inverted reflexes
concepts.body: In a C5–C6 cord lesion, tapping brachioradialis produces **no elbow flexion but brisk finger flexion**: the C6 arc is damaged (LMN at that level) while levels below are released (UMN). It marks the level of a cervical myelopathy.
concepts.ur: Inverted reflexes: C5–C6 cord lesion mein brachioradialis tap karne par elbow flexion nahi hoti magar fingers tezi se flex hoti hain: C6 arc kharab hai (us level par LMN) jabke neeche ke levels azad ho gaye (UMN). Yeh cervical myelopathy ke level ka nishan hai.

concepts.title: Localise with reflexes
concepts.body: Combine reflexes with tone, power and sensation.

head: Finding
Lesion
rows: Absent knee reflex + weak quads + medial leg numbness
Brisk legs, Babinski, normal arms, sensory level at T6
Brisk arms and legs, Hoffmann +, normal jaw jerk
Brisk reflexes everywhere + brisk jaw jerk
Absent reflexes acutely after cord injury
Spinal shock — UMN signs appear later

concepts.ur: Reflexes se localise karein: reflexes ko tone, power aur sensation ke saath mila kar dekhein. LMN lesion mein reflex kam, tone kam, wasting; UMN lesion mein reflex brisk, tone zyada, clonus aur Babinski.

concepts.title: Pitfalls
concepts.body: Anxious, young or athletic patients may have symmetrically brisk reflexes; older adults may lose the ankle reflexes normally. Asymmetry, associated weakness, clonus and Babinski matter far more than a single number.
concepts.ur: Ghaltiyan: ghabraye hue, jawan ya athletic patients mein reflexes dono sides symmetrically brisk ho sakte hain; buzurgon mein ankle reflexes normally gayab ho sakte hain. Asymmetry, saath ki kamzori, clonus aur Babinski ek akele number se kahin zyada ahem hain.

questions.prompt: Best position for the Achilles reflex in many patients?

Prone with the knee straight and foot pointed

questions.prompt: A positive Babinski sign is…
options: Toe flexion when the sole is stroked
Big-toe extension when the lateral sole is stroked
Knee extension when tapped
Ankle clonus
questions.explain: Extensor plantar response = UMN sign (abnormal after infancy).

questions.prompt: A Hoffmann sign is elicited by…

Squeezing the thumb
Flicking the nail of the middle finger downward
Tapping the biceps tendon

questions.prompt: Which hammer technique is correct?
options: Press the hammer slowly into the tendon
Hit as hard as possible
Tap the muscle belly only
Let the hammer swing freely from the wrist
questions.explain: A free swing delivers a brisk, consistent stretch.

questions.prompt: Absent ankle reflexes on both sides with numb feet suggest…
options: Bilateral L5 radiculopathy
Cervical myelopathy
Stroke
Peripheral polyneuropathy
questions.explain: Length-dependent neuropathy affects the longest nerves first.

questions.prompt: An inverted brachioradialis reflex suggests…
options: Carpal tunnel syndrome
A C8 radiculopathy
A C5–C6 cord lesion
Normal variation
questions.explain: LMN at C6 with UMN release below = cord lesion at C5–C6.

questions.prompt: Symmetrically brisk (3+) reflexes in an anxious 20-year-old with no other signs are…
options: Diagnostic of MS
Always a cord lesion
Possibly normal
A sign of neuropathy
questions.explain: Brisk but symmetrical reflexes without other UMN signs can be normal.

questions.prompt: Sustained ankle clonus is graded…
questions.explain: 4+ = very brisk with clonus.

questions.case: Clumsy hands, brisk biceps and knee reflexes, positive Hoffmann on both sides, normal jaw jerk.
questions.prompt: Most likely site?
options: Above the pons
Lumbar roots
Peripheral nerves
Cervical spinal cord
questions.explain: UMN signs in arms and legs with a normal jaw jerk = cervical cord.

questions.case: Day 1 after a complete T8 spinal cord injury: flaccid legs, absent reflexes.
questions.prompt: Explanation?
options: Spinal shock — reflexes return and become brisk over days to weeks
An additional peripheral nerve injury
Normal finding forever
Testing error
questions.explain: Spinal shock temporarily abolishes reflexes below the level.

questions.case: Absent right knee reflex, weak quadriceps 4/5, numb medial shin; hip adduction 4/5.
questions.prompt: Root or femoral nerve?
options: Femoral nerve only
Common fibular nerve
L4 (L3–L4) root — the adductors (obturator) are weak too
S1 root
questions.explain: Obturator-supplied adductors share L3–L4 but not the femoral nerve.

questions.case: Brisk reflexes in all limbs with a brisk jaw jerk and slurred speech.
questions.prompt: Lesion level?
options: Above the pons (e.g. bilateral cerebral or brainstem)
Peripheral nerve
Lumbar roots
Cervical cord
questions.explain: A brisk jaw jerk places the UMN lesion above the trigeminal motor nucleus.

questions.case: Back pain; absent left ankle reflex; weak calf raises on the left; numb lateral foot.
questions.prompt: Most likely level?
options: L4–L5 disc affecting L4
Cervical myelopathy
L3–L4 disc affecting L4
L5–S1 disc affecting the S1 root
questions.explain: A posterolateral L5–S1 disc compresses the traversing S1 root.

questions.case: Diabetes for 15 years; absent ankle reflexes, reduced knee reflexes, normal arms; numb feet to mid-shin.
questions.prompt: Interpretation?
options: Cauda equina syndrome
Bilateral S1 radiculopathy from two discs
Length-dependent sensorimotor polyneuropathy
Myelopathy
questions.explain: Distal-first symmetrical loss in a diabetic = polyneuropathy.

questions.case: Weak, wasted hand muscles with fasciculations, plus brisk reflexes and up-going plantars.
questions.prompt: What does the mix suggest?
options: Normal ageing
Combined UMN + LMN signs — consider motor neurone disease and refer to neurology
Carpal tunnel syndrome
Simple C8 radiculopathy
questions.explain: LMN signs (wasting, fasciculation) and UMN signs together, without sensory loss, raise concern for MND.

questions.case: A 70-year-old has symmetrically reduced ankle reflexes (1+) and no symptoms.
questions.prompt: What do you conclude?
options: Can be normal for age — interpret with symptoms and other findings
Needs emergency imaging
Spinal cord injury
Definite neuropathy
questions.explain: Ankle reflexes diminish with age; a single symmetric finding without symptoms is not a diagnosis.

questions.case: Positive Babinski on the right, brisk right biceps and knee reflexes, right arm drift.
questions.prompt: Where is the lesion?
options: Right cerebral hemisphere

Right lumbar roots
Left cerebral hemisphere or upper brainstem (contralateral UMN)
questions.explain: Right-sided UMN signs = left-sided lesion above the decussation.

Knee slightly flexed, support the leg; briskly dorsiflex the foot and hold it there.
Mouth slightly open; place a finger on the chin and tap it downward.
Stroke the lateral sole firmly with a blunt object from the heel toward the little toe, then across the ball of the foot.

questions.prompt: What is a positive Plantar response (Babinski sign)?

Rhythmic, repeated plantarflexion beats — sustained (more than about 3–5 beats) is abnormal
Flexion of the thumb and index finger
A brisk jaw closure

questions.prompt: What does an abnormal Plantar response (Babinski sign) suggest?
options: Upper motor neuron lesion; a few unsustained beats can be normal (especially if anxious).

stations.title: Upper- and lower-limb reflex screen
stations.scenario: Examine the deep tendon reflexes of a patient with back and neck pain, and report the grades.
tasks: Elicit biceps, brachioradialis, triceps, knee and ankle reflexes on both sides.
checklist: Positions each limb relaxed with the tendon on slight stretch
Elicits all five reflexes on both sides
Uses reinforcement for an absent reflex before calling it 0
States the root level of any abnormal reflex

stations.title: Screen for upper motor neuron signs
stations.scenario: A patient with progressive hand clumsiness. Screen for UMN signs.
checklist: Strokes the lateral sole from heel to little toe and across the ball of the foot
Flicks the middle-finger nail for Hoffmann
Briskly dorsiflexes and holds the foot for clonus
Counts beats and states sustained clonus is abnormal
Links findings to possible cervical myelopathy and urgent referral

cards.front: The Achilles reflex tests…
cards.back: S1. Ankle jerk = S1 (S1–S2).

cards.front: The triceps reflex tests…
cards.back: C7. Triceps = C7.

cards.front: A normal reflex is graded…
cards.back: 2+. 2+ = normal.

cards.front: Brisk reflexes suggest a lesion of the…
cards.back: Upper motor neuron. Loss of inhibition from above makes reflexes brisk.

cards.front: Which reflex is the only one for L5?
cards.back: Medial hamstring. Medial hamstring = L5.

cards.front: The Jendrassik manoeuvre is used to…
cards.back: Reinforce a weak or absent reflex. Pulling hooked fingers reinforces lower-limb reflexes.

cards.front: Best position for the Achilles reflex in many patients?
cards.back: Kneeling on a chair. Kneeling relaxes the calf and slightly pre-stretches the tendon.

cards.front: A positive Babinski sign is…
cards.back: Big-toe extension when the lateral sole is stroked. Extensor plantar response = UMN sign (abnormal after infancy).

cards.front: A Hoffmann sign is elicited by…
cards.back: Flicking the nail of the middle finger downward. Thumb and index flexion in response = positive.

cards.front: Which hammer technique is correct?
cards.back: Let the hammer swing freely from the wrist. A free swing delivers a brisk, consistent stretch.

cards.front: Absent ankle reflexes on both sides with numb feet suggest…
cards.back: Peripheral polyneuropathy. Length-dependent neuropathy affects the longest nerves first.

cards.front: An inverted brachioradialis reflex suggests…
cards.back: A C5–C6 cord lesion. LMN at C6 with UMN release below = cord lesion at C5–C6.

cards.front: Symmetrically brisk (3+) reflexes in an anxious 20-year-old with no other signs are…
cards.back: Possibly normal. Brisk but symmetrical reflexes without other UMN signs can be normal.

cards.front: Sustained ankle clonus is graded…
cards.back: 4+. 4+ = very brisk with clonus.

cards.front: Clumsy hands, brisk biceps and knee reflexes, positive Hoffmann on both sides, normal jaw jerk. — Most likely site?
cards.back: Cervical spinal cord. UMN signs in arms and legs with a normal jaw jerk = cervical cord.

cards.front: Day 1 after a complete T8 spinal cord injury: flaccid legs, absent reflexes. — Explanation?
cards.back: Spinal shock — reflexes return and become brisk over days to weeks. Spinal shock temporarily abolishes reflexes below the level.

cards.front: Absent right knee reflex, weak quadriceps 4/5, numb medial shin; hip adduction 4/5. — Root or femoral nerve?
cards.back: L4 (L3–L4) root — the adductors (obturator) are weak too. Obturator-supplied adductors share L3–L4 but not the femoral nerve.

cards.front: Brisk reflexes in all limbs with a brisk jaw jerk and slurred speech. — Lesion level?
cards.back: Above the pons (e.g. bilateral cerebral or brainstem). A brisk jaw jerk places the UMN lesion above the trigeminal motor nucleus.

cards.front: Back pain; absent left ankle reflex; weak calf raises on the left; numb lateral foot. — Most likely level?
cards.back: L5–S1 disc affecting the S1 root. A posterolateral L5–S1 disc compresses the traversing S1 root.

cards.front: Diabetes for 15 years; absent ankle reflexes, reduced knee reflexes, normal arms; numb feet to mid-shin. — Interpretation?
cards.back: Length-dependent sensorimotor polyneuropathy. Distal-first symmetrical loss in a diabetic = polyneuropathy.

cards.front: Weak, wasted hand muscles with fasciculations, plus brisk reflexes and up-going plantars. — What does the mix suggest?
cards.back: Combined UMN + LMN signs — consider motor neurone disease and refer to neurology. LMN signs (wasting, fasciculation) and UMN signs together, without sensory loss, raise concern for MND.

cards.front: A 70-year-old has symmetrically reduced ankle reflexes (1+) and no symptoms. — What do you conclude?
cards.back: Can be normal for age — interpret with symptoms and other findings. Ankle reflexes diminish with age; a single symmetric finding without symptoms is not a diagnosis.

cards.front: Positive Babinski on the right, brisk right biceps and knee reflexes, right arm drift. — Where is the lesion?
cards.back: Left cerebral hemisphere or upper brainstem (contralateral UMN). Right-sided UMN signs = left-sided lesion above the decussation.
